title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Protein Localization Prediction (E. coli)
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Protein Localization Prediction (E. coli)This dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_56 dataset, derived from the Ecoli (Imbalanced: 4) Dataset (KEEL Repository). The original data comprises 7 continuous features representing protein localization scores: Mcg, Gvh, Lip, Chg, Aac, Alm1, and Alm2. These scores correspond to different methods for predicting protein subcellular localization in the bacterium Escherichia coli. The target variable is Class, indicating whether the protein is localized in the outer membrane (om - positive class) or in other cellular locations (negative class). The dataset is significantly imbalanced (IR = 15.8), with only 5.95% positive instances, making it a classic benchmark for imbalanced classification research.Generation and Selection Methodology: The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where Random Oversampling was selected as the optimal technique), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the TVAE algorithm, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (8.097) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating superior preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 9,996 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 8 (7 predictive features + 1 target variable)Target Variable: Class (1 = Outer membrane localization - om, 0 = Other localization)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 1.100).Intended Use: This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for bioinformatics, protein localization prediction, and imbalanced classification. It is suitable for training and evaluating binary classification algorithms where accurate identification of outer membrane proteins is critical for understanding bacterial cell structure and function, particularly in gram-negative bacteria like E. coli. The significant class imbalance (originally 15.8:1) makes this dataset particularly valuable for evaluating techniques for imbalanced classification, including oversampling, undersampling, cost-sensitive learning, and ensemble methods. The synthetic nature of the data allows for safe sharing and benchmarking without concerns about biological data privacy.Protein Localization Scores (Features):Mcg: McGeoch method for signal sequence recognitionGvh: von Heijne method for signal sequence recognitionLip: von Heijne score for Signal Peptidase II prediction (often constant 0.48)Chg: Presence of charge in the N-terminal of predicted lipoproteins (often constant 0.5)Aac: Amino acid content discriminant analysis scoreAlm1: ALOM score for membrane region predictionAlm2: ALOM score excluding putative cleavable signal regionsClass Definitions:Positive Class (1): om - Outer membrane localization (5.95% of original)Negative Class (0): Other localizations including cp (Cytoplasm), im (Inner membrane), pp (Periplasm), etc. (94.05% of original)Performance Summary: Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.88, AUC-ROC of 0.07, and accuracy of 0.88. However, the original model failed completely to identify the minority class (outer membrane proteins), achieving precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.00 for the positive class. This is a classic example of the "accuracy paradox" in imbalanced classification. Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 1.00 (+0.12 improvement), AUC-ROC of 1.00 (+0.93 improvement), and accuracy of 1.00 (+0.12 improvement). The synthetic data achieved perfect classification performance, increasing precision from 0.00 to 1.00 (+1.00), recall from 0.00 to 1.00 (+1.00), and F1-score from 0.00 to 1.00 (+1.00) for the positive class. This demonstrates the exceptional effectiveness of the methodology in rescuing the model's ability to detect rare protein localizations, achieving perfect classification on the test set.Data Preprocessing Note: The original dataset (336 protein instances) was obtained from the KEEL Repository. The file was loaded by ignoring KEEL header lines and using comma as separator. Column names were assigned according to the documentation (Mcg, Gvh, Lip, Chg, Aac, Alm1, Alm2, Class). The target variable Class was mapped from 'positive' (om) to 1 and 'negative' (other localizations) to 0. Constant columns with zero variance (Lip and Chg, which are frequently constant in versions of this dataset) were identified and removed to prevent issues in correlation calculations and machine learning models. No additional scaling was applied as all features are already in the range [0, 1].Imbalanced Classification Significance: The Ecoli imbalanced dataset is a classic benchmark in imbalanced classification research, widely used for:Evaluating and comparing oversampling/undersampling techniquesTesting cost-sensitive learning methodsValidating ensemble methods for imbalanced dataDemonstrating the "accuracy paradox" where high accuracy masks poor minority class performanceResearch in bioinformatics and protein localization predictionPrivacy and Ethics: The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real protein sequences that could be traced to specific organisms beyond the bacterium Escherichia coli. The original dataset contains no personally identifiable information. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). The results showed a neutral risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.509, near random guessing), and zero exact copies were generated, making this dataset suitable for broader research sharing, while acknowledging that perfect privacy cannot be guaranteed and use should be governed by ethical guidelines for synthetic biological data.Related Work: This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for bioinformatics and imbalanced classification applications. For more details on the methodology and additional datasets, please visit the project's companion website: https://mdiazbastida.github.io/codigomdb/investigaciones.html

title: [Depreciated and replaced by V3] From the Self-Proven Theorem to Master-Level Chess - and the Law Inside Neural Networks
abstract: [Depreciated and replaced by V3] The application-specific clean rebuild has not yet been published; its authoritative theoretical boundary is now the governing V3 branch: After Turing: The Fold Machine - An Exact, Parameter-Free and Machine-Closed Derivation of Classical Computational Science from Smithian Fold Theory. The V3 source platform is https://github.com/MettaMazza/ernos-labs-sft-platform. The original DOI, concept DOI, version number and files are preserved for transparent historical provenance; this record must not be presented or cited as current V3 work. Derived law has now secured the Stockfish ladder through Elo 1900. FoldBot is a complete chess engine with zero learned weights, tuned piece values, opening book, or training: material is counted from live board geometry, position value is an exact rational share of the One, and minimax is the fold's complement. The pinned campaign secures 1700 at 54.2% and 1900 at 62.5% (6W-3D-3L) with externally refereed legality. The v20/current calculation continuation preserves every legal root move to common depth, proves 4/4 sequential/parallel move identity and 4/4 exact-value identity, derives worker messages from the supplied ceiling, and owns table addressing through live capacities. Current and pinned v20 agree on 36/36 real 2100 positions at ceiling 3; the current engine completes the same panel at depths 8-11. The 2100 rung remains the active greater-than-50-percent benchmark-victory objective under Maria Smith's authority to designate the real run and publish its conclusion. The secured 1900 victory, exact legality and endgame proofs, common-depth identity, and demonstrated real-position calculation establish a constructive route forward; no theorem-derived wall has been produced. The companion neural-weight and fold-native language results support the wider proposition: much of what computation purchases with parameters is law, and law can be derived.

title: Computational Algebra, Coding Theory and Cryptography
abstract: This Special Issue focuses on recent developments in algebraic approaches to coding theory and cryptography, particularly on new encoding and decoding methods derived from different algebraic structures. The Issue emphasizes the use of algebraic techniques to design algorithms capable of improving error-correction performance as well as the efficiency of encoding and decoding procedures.The algebraic structures considered include commutative, computational, ordered, and hypercompositional algebras, together with their interactions with combinatorial methods and related areas such as lattice theory, category theory, graph theory, and mathematical modeling. Particular attention is given to both theoretical foundations and modern applications of these structures in error-control codes and cryptographic systems.

title: AI, Brain Death Detection, and Islamic Law
abstract: The deployment of machine learning systems capable of detecting covert consciousness in neurologically injured patients creates a profound challenge at the intersection of clinical medicine, AI ethics, and Islamic jurisprudence. We argue that the shift from binary clinical verdicts to probabilistic, temporally granular neural-state estimates should be addressed through three foundational constructs in Islamic legal epistemology: bayyina (clear evidentiary proof), yaqin (epistemic certainty), and the theologically mandated agnosticism about there (soul). We survey the current technical literature on AI-based consciousness detection, map it onto the landscape of Islamic brain death scholarship, and identifykey challenges. We also discuss its implications for AI surrogate decision systems.

title: Switch-Reasoner: Learn When to Think in Multitask Mixtures via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often follow a fixed Think-then-Answer paradigm, which is inefficient in heterogeneous multitask settings because simple inputs may not require explicit reasoning while difficult ones can benefit substantially from it. Learning when to think is also unstable during post-training, where imbalanced rollouts can drive the model toward always-thinking or always-direct behavior. We propose Switch-Reasoner, a GRPO-based framework that learns to adaptively select reasoning modes for MLLMs. It treats thinking as a virtual tool invocation and allows the model to either answer directly or invoke explicit reasoning before answering. To stabilize this decision, we introduce a dual-level regulation mechanism that balances the overall use of Thinking Mode and Direct Mode while providing sample-level supervision based on the relative benefit of the two choices. Experiments on 11 multimodal tasks show that Switch-Reasoner reduces unnecessary reasoning while maintaining strong performance, achieving a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

evidence.title: Switch-Reasoner: Learn When to Think in Multitask Mixtures via Reinforcement Learning
evidence.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often follow a fixed Think-then-Answer paradigm, which is inefficient in heterogeneous multitask settings because simple inputs may not require explicit reasoning while difficult ones can benefit substantially from it. Learning when to think is also unstable during post-training, where imbalanced rollouts can drive the model toward always-thinking or always-direct behavior. We propose Switch-Reasoner, a GRPO-based framework that learns to adaptively select reasoning modes for MLLMs. It treats thinking as a virtual tool invocation and allows the model to either answer directly or invoke explicit reasoning before answering. Experiments on 11 multimodal tasks show that Switch-Reasoner reduces unnecessary reasoning while maintaining strong performance, achieving a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

title: El Transformer y la revolución de la atención
abstract: Este Trabajo de Fin de Grado estudia la arquitectura Transformer como uno de los avances más relevantes del aprendizaje profundo moderno. El trabajo comienza contextualizando su aparición a partir de las limitaciones de las redes recurrentes, las LSTM y los modelos convolucionales aplicados a datos secuenciales, especialmente en relación con las dependencias de largo alcance, la propagación del gradiente y la limitada paralelización. A continuación, se presentan los principales componentes matemáticos y arquitectónicos del Transformer: embeddings, codificación posicional, mecanismo de autoatención mediante queries, keys y values, atención multi-cabeza, redes feed-forward, conexiones residuales y normalización. También se analiza el flujo de información en modelos encoder, decoder y encoder–decoder, relacionando estas estructuras con sistemas representativos como BERT, GPT, T5 y BART. Además, se explica el papel del aprendizaje autosupervisado, el transfer learning y las leyes de escala en el desarrollo de los grandes modelos de lenguaje. El estudio aborda también el problema de la eficiencia computacional mediante una introducción a las técnicas de cuantización aplicadas a grandes modelos de lenguaje y una comparación práctica entre un modelo en FP16 y una versión cuantizada mediante AWQ INT4, analizando el consumo de memoria, el tamaño de almacenamiento, el tiempo de carga, la velocidad de generación y la calidad del modelo. Finalmente, el trabajo amplía su alcance más allá del procesamiento del lenguaje natural, abordando aplicaciones en visión, audio, sistemas multimodales y biología computacional. También se exponen algunas de las principales limitaciones actuales, como el coste computacional cuadrático, las alucinaciones, los sesgos y la dependencia de grandes volúmenes de datos, así como posibles líneas futuras basadas en atención eficiente, arquitecturas alternativas y agentes con uso de herramientas. Los anexos complementan la memoria con los fundamentos matemáticos necesarios para comprender la arquitectura y su entrenamiento. Abstract: This Final Degree Project studies the Transformer architecture as one of the most influential advances in modern deep learning. The work begins by contextualizing its emergence from the limitations of recurrent neural networks, LSTMs and convolutional approaches applied to sequential data, particularly regarding long-range dependencies, gradient propagation and limited parallelization. It then presents the main mathematical and architectural components of Transformers: embeddings, positional encoding, self-attention through queries, keys and values, multi-head attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections and normalization. The project also analyses the flow of information in encoder, decoder and encoder–decoder models, relating these structures to representative systems such as BERT, GPT, T5 and BART. In addition, it explains the role of self-supervised learning, transfer learning and scaling laws in the development of large language models. The study also addresses the problem of computational efficiency through an introduction to quantization techniques for large language models and a practical comparison between an FP16 model and an AWQ INT4 quantized version, analysing memory consumption, storage size, loading time, generation speed and model quality. Finally, the scope of the study extends beyond natural language processing, covering applications in vision, audio, multimodal systems and computational biology. The work discusses current limitations, including quadratic computational cost, hallucinations, bias and dependence on large-scale data, as well as future directions based on efficient attention, alternative architectures and tool-using agents. The annexes complement the main text with the mathematical foundations required to understand the architecture and its training.

title: Dendritic Wave Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract Wave recurrent neural networks (wRNNs) are biologically inspired recurrent architectures that use traveling-wave dynamics to support sequence learning and memory. However, their input-to-hidden pathway remains relatively simple compared with biological neurons, where dendrites perform nonlinear input integration. In this study, we introduce the Dendritic Wave Recurrent Neural Network (DW-RNN), which augments the input pathway of the wRNN with nonlinear basal dendritic branches while preserving the original recurrent wave dynamics. We evaluate DW-RNN on a simple copy task, sequential MNIST (sMNIST), permuted sequential MNIST (psMNIST), and noisy sequential CIFAR-10 (nsCIFAR-10). On the copy task, DW-RNN shows learning behavior comparable to the standard wRNN, suggesting that dendritic input integration does not disrupt the recurrent wave-based memory mechanism. On the three sequential image-classification benchmarks, DW-RNN outperforms the standard wRNN, improving accuracy from 97.27 ± 0.15% to 97.82 ± 0.12% on sMNIST, from 96.74 ± 0.17% to 96.92 ± 0.10% on psMNIST, and from 54.30 ± 0.79% to 55.65 ± 0.55% on nsCIFAR-10. In addition to improving mean accuracy, DW-RNN exhibits lower across-seed variability on all three classification benchmarks, suggesting that dendritic input integration may improve the stability of wRNN training. Hidden-activity visualizations further show that DW-RNN preserves the characteristic traveling-wave patterns of the original wRNN. These results suggest that dendritic computation and traveling-wave recurrent dynamics provide complementary mechanisms for biologically inspired sequence learning.

title: CATS 2.0: Leveraging Large Language Models and Graph Databases for Robust Arabic SMS E-Commerce Systems
abstract: Arabic SMS-based e-commerce platforms pose unique challenges due to the spontaneous and noisy nature of user-generated text (e.g., abbreviations, dialectal Arabic, or “Arabizi” transliterations). In this paper, we present Classified Ads Text Service (CATS) 2.0, an improved classified ads system that combines probabilistic large language models (LLMs) with deterministic graph-based knowledge representations to achieve robust understanding and matching of Arabic SMS content. Building on earlier work that emphasized the importance of integrating sublanguage analysis with content-oriented methods, our approach uses a hybrid pipeline: an LLM interprets free-text messages and extracts structured information, which is then inserted into a Neo4j graph database representing the domain knowledge. This graph-based representation enables precise semantic matching of “selling” and “looking for” posts and supports reasoning over the ads network. We evaluate the system on real-world Arabic SMS e-commerce data. Experimental results show that the hybrid CATS 2.0 system achieves high accuracy in content extraction (improving the F-measure over the original system’s ~90%) and successfully handles multilingual and transliterated inputs. The proposed approach demonstrates how coupling an LLM’s flexibility with a knowledge graph’s rigor can substantially enhance the robustness and extensibility of e-commerce text processing in Arabic.

title: Fuzzy Logic-based Approaches
abstract: Fuzzy logic-based methods have found good applications in industrial control systems, some home appliances (e.g., washing machine), robotics, and aerospace engineering. At the outset the conventional control system can be just regarded as a (minimally-)intelligent control/system, if at least, it uses fuzzy logic (or some other logic), and/or uses some learning mechanism. If, say y > some number, then use one controller or else use another one – this is a conditional logic. Actually the artificial intelligent (AI-based) system should have strong logic capability and very good learning/adaptive mechanisms. A fuzzy logic (FL)-based controller is suited to keep: i) output variable/s between the limits, and ii) control actuation (either control input or related variable) between the limits. Thus, FL is one form of logic that can be used in the design and operation of an intelligent control as one component of AI. FL deals with vagueness rather than uncertainty: if a patient has a ‘severe’ headache, then there is a ‘good chance’ that she/he has a migraine. To avoid contradictions in the rules some human intervention is sometimes needed at certain stages to tune various adjustable parameters in the FL system and rule base, because the FL-based systems depend on a specified rule base. The FL-based control is suitable when: i) control system dynamics are slow and/or nonlinear, ii) the mathematical models of the plant are not available, and iii) competent human operators who would provide expert operational rules are available.

title: High Energy Photon Polarimetry at Lepton Colliders: Quantum Information from Converted Photons
abstract: We study high-energy photons produced at a lepton collider that convert into an $e^+e^-$ pair in the detector, as a tool for measuring quantum information observables. We consider single- and double-conversion processes in $e^+e^- \to γγ$ and $e^+e^- \to e^+e^-γ$. Single conversions enable an in situ extraction of the spin-analyzing power, while double conversions probe polarization correlations. Focusing on the Belle-II detector, we show that, depending on the reconstruction resolution of the opening angle of the conversion $e^+e^-$ pair, quantum correlations of the diphoton system can be probed. In particular, measurements of violations of the Bell inequality, quantum discord, concurrence, nonstabilizerness, and steerability with spatially separated GeV-scale photons can be made at high significance.

title: Robust Heteroskedastic Matrix Factorization: A Generalization of PCA that Flags Outliers and Handles Missing Data
abstract: We present Robust Heteroskedastic Matrix Factorization (RHMF), a generalization of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) that is robust to outliers, handles per-feature uncertainties and missing data, and automatically flags per-feature and per-object anomalies. RHMF is useful both in recovering a low-dimensional embedding unspoiled by bad data or anomalies, and in identifying those anomalies. It utilises an iterative reweighting algorithm that implicitly maximizes a Student-t likelihood. This admits an equivalent probabilistic interpretation as fitting a hierarchical model with per-data-point latent variances. We deliver a fast JAX implementation, Robusta-HMF, and practical guidance for users. We demonstrate the ability of the model to identify and mitigate outliers of different classes. Identification accuracy is contingent on the choice of hyperparameters, but we show that these can be set reliably by cross-validation. We also apply RHMF to RVS spectra from Gaia DR3 to find main-sequence stars that are strange relative to their neighbors in color-magnitude space. We highlight specific examples, including a known binary hosting a Be star, and M-dwarfs with subtle emission in the Ca II triplet lines, indicative of accretion or magnetic activity, which would not be obvious to identify by eye.

title: Structured Pruning of Large Language Models via Power Transformation and Sign-Preserving Score Aggregation with Adaptive Feature Retention
abstract: This paper proposes an improved structured pruning method for large language models (LLMs) that addresses key challenges in adapting Adaptive Feature Retention (AFR), an unstructured pruning technique, to structured pruning. When applying AFR to structured pruning, three major problems arise: distribution mismatch between heterogeneous pruning scores, loss of sign information indicating optimization direction consistency, and influence of outliers. To address these issues, we propose a unified approach combining power transformation for nonlinear distribution alignment, sign-preserving score aggregation, and percentile-based outlier removal. Experiments on Llama-3-8B, Vicuna-v1.5-13B, and LLaVA-v1.5-13B demonstrate that our method maintains accuracy comparable to unstructured pruning while achieving practical inference speedup through structured pruning.

title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Credit Risk Assessment
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Credit Risk Assessment (German Credit Data)This dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_42 dataset, derived from the Statlog (German Credit Data) Dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository). The original data comprises 20 attributes describing the creditworthiness of bank customers, including sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, marital status, employment, housing), financial information (checking account status, savings, credit amount, duration, installment rate), and credit history. The target variable is risk_bad, indicating whether a customer is a good (0) or bad (1) credit risk.Generation and Selection Methodology: The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where Smote was selected as the optimal technique), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the SMOTE RSB + Ruido Gaussiano* algorithm, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (9.985) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating superior preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 9,656 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 21 (20 predictive features + 1 target variable)Target Variable: risk_bad (1 = Bad credit risk, 0 = Good credit risk)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 1.069).Intended Use: This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for credit scoring, risk assessment, and financial decision-making. It is suitable for training and evaluating binary classification algorithms where accurate identification of high-risk borrowers is critical for minimizing financial losses. The synthetic nature of the data allows for safe sharing and benchmarking without exposing potentially sensitive financial information from real bank customers.Performance Summary: Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.70, AUC-ROC of 0.76, and accuracy of 0.72. The original model showed moderate performance on the minority class (bad credit risk), with precision of 0.55, recall of 0.35, and an F1-score of 0.43. Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.75 (+0.05 improvement), AUC-ROC of 0.78 (+0.02 improvement), and accuracy of 0.74 (+0.02 improvement). The synthetic data significantly improved the minority class performance, increasing precision from 0.55 to 0.57 (+0.02), recall from 0.35 to 0.62 (+0.27), and F1-score from 0.43 to 0.59 (+0.16). This demonstrates the effectiveness of the methodology in capturing complex financial patterns and enhancing the detection of high-risk borrowers.Data Preprocessing Note: The original dataset (1,000 credit applications) was obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. The original class variable (1 = Good, 2 = Bad) was transformed into a binary target (risk_bad) with 1 indicating bad credit risk and 0 indicating good credit risk. Three ordinal variables were coded preserving their hierarchical structure: checking_status (1-4, from negative balance to no account), savings_status (0-4, from unknown to high savings), and employment (0-4, from unemployed to ≥7 years). Ten nominal variables were label-encoded. All variables were converted to integer type for consistency. A stratified subsample of the original dataset was created for efficient experimentation while preserving the original class distribution (~70% good credit / ~30% bad credit).Privacy and Ethics: The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real customer financial records that could be traced to specific individuals. While the original dataset contains demographic information (age, sex, marital status, nationality), the synthetic generation process ensures that no real individual can be re-identified. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). The results showed a neutral risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.500, exactly at random guessing), and a limited number of exact copies (91 records), making this dataset suitable for broader research sharing, while acknowledging that perfect privacy cannot be guaranteed and use should be governed by ethical guidelines for synthetic financial data.Related Work: This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for financial and risk assessment applications. For more details on the methodology and additional datasets, please visit the project's companion website: https://mdiazbastida.github.io/codigomdb/investigaciones.html

The synthetic data significantly improved the minority class performance, increasing precision from 0.55 to 0.57 (+0.02), recall from 0.35 to 0.62 (+0.27), and F1-score from 0.43 to 0.59 (+0.16). This demonstrates the effectiveness of the methodology in capturing complex financial patterns and enhancing the detection of high-risk borrowers.Data Preprocessing Note: The original dataset (1,000 credit applications) was obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. The original class variable (1 = Good, 2 = Bad) was transformed into a binary target (risk_bad) with 1 indicating bad credit risk and 0 indicating good credit risk. Three ordinal variables were coded preserving their hierarchical structure: checking_status (1-4, from negative balance to no account), savings_status (0-4, from unknown to high savings), and employment (0-4, from unemployed to ≥7 years). Ten nominal variables were label-encoded. All variables were converted to integer type for consistency. A stratified subsample of the original dataset was created for efficient experimentation while preserving the original class distribution (~70% good credit / ~30% bad credit).Privacy and Ethics: The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real customer financial records that could be traced to specific individuals. While the original dataset contains demographic information (age, sex, marital status, nationality), the synthetic generation process ensures that no real individual can be re-identified. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). The results showed a neutral risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.500, exactly at random guessing), and a limited number of exact copies (91 records), making this dataset suitable for broader research sharing, while acknowledging that perfect privacy cannot be guaranteed and use should be governed by ethical guidelines for synthetic financial data.Related Work: This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for financial and risk assessment applications. For more details on the methodology and additional datasets, please visit the project's companion website: https://mdiazbastida.github.io/codigomdb/investigaciones.html

title: AI-Powered Customer Feedback Analytics & Rating Engine Using NLP
abstract: The modern world is filled with stress. A person's pressure is affected by a variety of factors. Representatives in IT are more likely to be under pressure due to work pressure, overburdening, higher worker mastery, and so on. When a person is stressed, it can lead to a variety of mental health issues such as depression, anxiety, somatization, lack of concentration, and so on. As a result, it is necessary to identify human stress at an early stage in order to provide appropriate solutions and alleviate stress. There has been a lot of research done on stress prediction. Many research papers use Machine Learning techniques to predict stress, and many papers use IOT based sensors to extract the features needed for stress prediction. There are so many existing systems in predicting employee stress. In this project we are going to predict the employee stress using XGBOOST algorithm since it gives more Accuracy. Based on this the prediction we will remediate the persons under stress in the early stage which is good for their health and as well as the work. Keywords: Natural Language Processing, TF-IDF, Logistic Regression, Sentiment Analysis, Machine Learning

abstract: This record provides the clean supplementary dataset, model, and mapping-result package for the manuscript "Mapping Hydrated Minerals in Chryse Planitia, Mars via a Meteorite-Constrained CNN-Transformer Architecture: Revealing Fine-Scale Aqueous Alteration Records". title: Stitching It Together The Enemies of Sackboy
abstract: Enemies are not usually the main focus of platformers, so are often quite simplistic, and while the enemies in Sackboy: A Big Adventure are on the more complex side for platformers, the amount of system complexity required to make them responsive, reliable and robust may still surprise. This chapter gives an overview of some of the technologies and systems behind the enemies and bosses in Sackboy: A Big Adventure , as well as some of the challenges that were encountered during development. Some key areas are how the targeting and detection systems were created, as well as various other systems (such as for coordinating attacks and for keeping enemies out of each other’s way).

title: Deep learning integration of initial abdominal radiography and early clinical information for predicting hospitalization of patients with abdominal symptoms
abstract: Abdominal symptoms are a common reason for emergency department visits, yet early admission decisions remain challenging due to limited diagnostic information available at the initial stage of evaluation. Abdominal radiography is frequently performed as a first-line imaging modality, but its role in supporting early hospitalization decisions remains underexplored. In this study, we propose a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates abdominal radiographs with early clinical information to predict hospitalization outcomes. Convolutional neural networks were used to extract imaging features, while language models were applied to encode clinical text information. These features were combined through a fusion layer to perform admission versus discharge classification. The proposed framework was evaluated using multiple deep learning architectures paired with classical machine learning classifiers. Experimental results demonstrate that the multimodal approach outperforms single-modality models. The best-performing configuration achieved area under the ROC curve (AUC) values of 0.7958 and 0.8638 before and after data augmentation, respectively. These findings suggest that integrating abdominal imaging with early clinical information can improve predictive performance and may support clinical decision-making in emergency care settings.

title: A Step Forward Towards Trustworthy Risk-Aware Facial Retrieval (RA-FR)
abstract: Facial image retrieval in unconstrained surveillance environments is a high-stakes challenge where missing a subject of interest -- a single false negative -- is simply not an option. Despite near-perfect performance on curated benchmarks, current recognition systems falter under real-world domain shifts such as low resolution, motion blur, and uncontrolled illumination (e.g., SCFace). Addressing this reliability gap, we propose Risk-Aware Facial Retrieval (RA-FR), a framework that moves beyond fixed Top-$k$ retrieval to adaptive set generation, guaranteeing ground truth inclusion within a user-specified risk level ($α$) and confidence level ($1 - δ$). Our approach integrates three core contributions: (1) reducing aleatoric uncertainty via a hybrid blind face restoration technique coupling Latent Consistency Models (InterLCM) and DiffBIR; (2) extracting discriminative, restoration-robust features via self-supervised DINOv1 ViT-B with GGeM pooling; and (3) employing conformal prediction with Hoeffding's inequality to dynamically calibrate retrieval set sizes based on query uncertainty. On the IMFDB benchmark, it consistently satisfies a 5% risk target with an average retrieval set size of approximately 10 images. By unifying domain-specific restoration, robust representation learning, and provable decision rules, RA-FR offers a pipeline that makes facial retrieval in surveillance both reliable and auditable. The code is available at: https://github.com/MuhammadEmmadSiddiqui/RA-FR.

title: A Nonstabilizerness Resource Law for Universal Quantum State Purification
abstract: Quantum state purification aims to recover higher-fidelity quantum states from multiple noisy copies and is a fundamental primitive for quantum information processing. Magic resources enable operations beyond classically simulable dynamics and are central to universal fault-tolerant quantum computation. Recent no-go results show that classically simulable operations cannot achieve a nontrivial universal fidelity gain. This motivates a quantitative theory of the magic required for purification at prescribed success probability and target fidelity. For universal purification with two input copies, we prove an exact linear mana law in odd dimensions and a two-sided linear robustness law for multi-qubit systems, which becomes exact for a single qubit. We also identify an explicit successful purification map that makes the tradeoff transparent. These results establish universal purification as a task obeying a quantitative magic-fidelity law and link magic resources to error mitigation and fault-tolerant quantum information processing.

title: Early to Share, Late to Save: Synchronisation-Driven Communication Gating in Bandwidth-Constrained Cooperative VLN
abstract: Most cooperative Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) methods assume unlimited communication, not considering real-world applications where bandwidth is restricted and information efficiency is critical. We introduce \textbf{bandwidth-constrained cooperative VLN} and propose \textbf{hindsight gating}: a lightweight supervised gate that labels communication-critical steps post-hoc from navigation failures, avoiding the high variance of REINFORCE. Contrary to the intuition that agents should communicate when uncertain, we observe a consistent counter-intuitive pattern: trained gates fire predominantly in early episode steps and more often when agents are confident, across all budget levels ($B \in \{1,3,5\}$). We explain this through \textbf{recurrent hidden-state alignment}: early communication injects grounded trajectory representations that persist and compound through subsequent Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) updates, achieving $+0.072$ cumulative alignment gain with $B{=}3$ transmissions, approaching unconstrained communication ($+0.078$) at 260\% greater alignment efficiency than random gating ($+0.020$) and 320\% greater efficiency than entropy-based gating ($+0.017$). Our results establish a new communication regime for bandwidth-limited embodied agents: synchronise representations early, navigate independently later. Our codebase is available at: https://github.com/AravG13/bandwidth-constrained-cooperative-vln

title: PGD-NO: A Neural Operator with Precomputed Geometry Decomposition for 3D Million-scale Physics Simulations
abstract: While neural PDE solvers have demonstrated significant potential for accelerating engineering simulations, existing architectures remain constrained by high memory consumption and the single node bottleneck, where the maximum processable mesh resolution is strictly limited by the VRAM of a single compute unit. To address these challenges, we propose PGD-NO, a neural operator with Precomputed Geometry Decomposition, that relocates the computational overhead of geometric encoding to a deterministic pre-computation phase. By utilizing an iterative geometry decomposition algorithm to extract geometry tokens, our model decouples feature extraction from solution querying. This architecture enables linear memory scalability, allowing high fidelity learning on meshes exceeding 10 million nodes, a scale where existing architectures typically encounter memory exhaustion. PGD-NO demonstrates competitive predictive accuracy across diverse industrial benchmarks and provides intrinsic interpretability through attention mechanisms. By effectively overcoming traditional mesh-size constraints, PGD-NO offers a robust and efficient solution for the next generation of large-scale, high-fidelity industrial design applications.

title: Sistema de detección de anomalías en series temporales para procesos de soldadura láser
abstract: Este Trabajo Fin de Máster aborda la detección de anomalías en series temporales procedentes de un proceso industrial de soldadura láser. En líneas de producción de alta cadencia, los fallos de soldadura generan piezas defectuosas que solo se detectan tras el evento, sin posibilidad de intervención preventiva. El reto consiste en identificar patrones de degradación en las curvas de proceso (fuerza, desplazamiento total del motor, potencia láser y desplazamiento de soldadura) antes de que ocurra el fallo, permitiendo al operario actuar con antelación. Los datos provienen de una estación de soldadura con cuatro tool positions que procesan dos familias de producto (MMxKb y MMxStd), con tasas de fallo inferiores al 1%, lo que convierte el problema en detección de anomalías bajo desbalanceo extremo. El objetivo principal es diseñar un sistema de detección de pre-fallos basado en autoencoders que supere a los métodos clásicos. Los objetivos específicos incluyen comparar múltiples arquitecturas (Dense, LSTM, GRU, Conv1D, Transformer) y evaluar operacionalmente el sistema con métricas interpretables para producción. Los baselines clásicos (Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, LOF) operan sobre curvas aplanadas de 256 dimensiones sin explotar la estructura temporal. El mejor baseline es OC-SVM con AUROC medio de 0,665 y Average Precision inferior a 0,06. En la comparación de autoencoders con 50 000 muestras, GRU AE domina en MMxKb (AUROC = 0,764, AP = 0,084, F1 = 0,215), mientras que en MMxStd empatan LSTM AE y Dense AE (rank = 1,62), resolviéndose a favor de LSTM AE tras entrenamiento con datos completos. La evaluación operacional a 20 falsas alarmas por día muestra que en MMxKb se detecta el 58,8% de las piezas en ventana de pre-fallo (OC-SVM) y en MMxStd el 72,3% (GRU AE), con el autoencoder seleccionado alcanzando el 52,9% y el 70,8% respectivamente. El lead time mediano es de 4 piezas antes del fallo (equivalente a ≈12 s; ciclo ≈3 s/pieza), con detección del 93,5% y 94,7% de los eventos de burst a umbral P90 en MMxKb y MMxStd respectivamente. El análisis por señal revela perfiles diferenciados: en MMxKb la potencia láser domina (AUROC = 0,683, ratio de error 3,1×), mientras que en MMxStd todas las señales contribuyen de forma equilibrada (AUROC entre 0,636 y 0,682). La anomalía se concentra en la fase early del proceso (primeros 25% del ciclo) en ambas familias. La evaluación bootstrap con 1 000 iteraciones confirma la estabilidad: MMxKb GRU AE alcanza AUROC = 0,777 (IC 95 %: [0,760; 0,795]); MMxStd LSTM AE alcanza AUROC = 0,698 (IC 95 %: [0,681; 0,714]). El sistema demuestra que los autoencoders superan significativamente a los métodos clásicos en la detección de pre-fallos en soldadura láser. La selección per-family es esencial dado que ninguna arquitectura domina universalmente. El hallazgo más relevante operacionalmente es que el sistema proporciona anticipación real al fallo con lead times medianos de ≈12 s (4 piezas). La explicabilidad por señal y región temporal permite al operario comprender la alerta sin interpretar puntuaciones numéricas. Abstract: This Master’s Thesis addresses anomaly detection in time series from an industrial laser welding process. In high-cadence production lines, welding failures produce defective parts that are only detected after the event, with no opportunity for preventive intervention. The challenge consists in identifying degradation patterns in process curves (force, total motor displacement, laser power, and welding displacement) before a failure occurs, enabling the operator to act in advance. Data come from a welding station with four tool positions processing two product families (MMxKb and MMxStd), with failure rates below 1%, which frames the problem as anomaly detection under extreme class imbalance. The main objective is to design a pre-failure detection system based on autoencoders that outperforms classical anomaly detection methods. Specific objectives include comparing multiple architectures (Dense, LSTM, GRU, Conv1D, Transformer) and operationally evaluating the system using production-interpretable metrics. Classical baselines (Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, LOF) operate on flattened curves of 256 dimensions without exploiting temporal structure. The best baseline is OC-SVM with a mean AUROC of 0.665 and Average Precision below 0.06. In the autoencoder comparison on 50 000 samples, GRU AE dominates in MMxKb (AUROC = 0.764, AP = 0.084, F1 = 0.215), while in MMxStd the LSTM AE and Dense AE tie (rank = 1.62), resolved in favour of LSTM AE after training on the full dataset. The operational evaluation at 20 false alarms per day shows that in MMxKb, 58.8% of the pre-failure window parts are detected (OC-SVM) and in MMxStd 72.3% (GRU AE), with the selected autoencoder achieving 52.9% and 70.8% respectively. The median lead time is 4 parts before failure (equivalent to ≈12 s; cycle ≈3 s/part), with 93.5% and 94.7% of burst events detected at the P90 threshold in MMxKb and MMxStd respectively. Signal-level analysis reveals differentiated profiles: in MMxKb laser power dominates (AUROC = 0.683, error ratio 3.1×), whereas in MMxStd all signals contribute equally (AUROC between 0.636 and 0.682). The anomaly concentrates in the early phase of the process (first 25% of the cycle) in both families. Bootstrap evaluation with 1 000 iterations confirms stability: MMxKb GRU AE achieves AUROC = 0.777 (95% CI: [0.760; 0.795]); MMxStd LSTM AE achieves AUROC = 0.698 (95% CI: [0.681; 0.714]). The system demonstrates that autoencoders significantly outperform classical methods in pre-failure detection for laser welding. Per-family model selection is essential, as no single architecture dominates universally. The most operationally relevant finding is that the system provides genuine anticipation of failure with median lead times of ≈12 s (4 parts). Signal-level and temporal-region explainability allows the operator to understand each alert without interpreting numerical scores.

The median lead time is 4 parts before failure (equivalent to ≈12 s; cycle ≈3 s/part), with 93.5% and 94.7% of burst events detected at the P90 threshold in MMxKb and MMxStd respectively. Signal-level analysis reveals differentiated profiles: in MMxKb laser power dominates (AUROC = 0.683, error ratio 3.1×), whereas in MMxStd all signals contribute equally (AUROC between 0.636 and 0.682). The anomaly concentrates in the early phase of the process (first 25% of the cycle) in both families. Bootstrap evaluation with 1 000 iterations confirms stability: MMxKb GRU AE achieves AUROC = 0.777 (95% CI: [0.760; 0.795]); MMxStd LSTM AE achieves AUROC = 0.698 (95% CI: [0.681; 0.714]). The system demonstrates that autoencoders significantly outperform classical methods in pre-failure detection for laser welding. Per-family model selection is essential, as no single architecture dominates universally. The most operationally relevant finding is that the system provides genuine anticipation of failure with median lead times of ≈12 s (4 parts). Signal-level and temporal-region explainability allows the operator to understand each alert without interpreting numerical scores.

title: Resolution Cost of Structured Inquiry States: Mechanism Dependence in the Energy-Bridge Test
abstract: Q-Bridge is a validation suite for testing whether structured inquiry states can be formally represented, constrained, measured, and evaluated as unresolved state-space configurations. The suite tests a sequence in which a state of affairs becomes an object of inquiry, activates primitive interrogative dimensions, forms a structured question-state, becomes measurable as a configuration, expands when dimensions remain unresolved, and requires resolution to reduce that unresolved state-space. The energy-bridge question enters at the final step: whether resolution cost scales with unresolved interrogative structure rather than with surface-level confounds. This paper reports the completed energy-bridge results across two generations of the experiment. The first generation, spanning standard LLM generation, answer-length-controlled generation, reasoning-mode generation, and exhaustive enumeration over the declared candidate space, established mechanism dependence: generative LLM resolution showed no positive dependence of cost on unresolved interrogative structure, reasoning-mode generation showed a significant negative dependence later sharpened by reconciliation tests, and exhaustive enumeration showed constructive scaling with an arbitrary-kernel marginal constant of approximately 2.2 mJ per candidate. The second generation removed that generation's central caveat. A preregistered campaign with three analytic runs and one exact repetition replaced the arbitrary SHA-256 kernel with SAT, under which the unresolved interrogative bits are the free variables and the solver's work is the resolution itself. On an uncontaminated CPU channel, energy tracked genuine constraint resolution at r = 0.99 for both exhaustive checking and conflict-driven pruned search, cost peaked at the satisfiability phase transition, and the marginal constant fell to 0.032 to 0.043 mJ per satisfaction check, superseding the arbitrary-kernel value. The campaign's negative control caught a GPU contamination that had inflated combined-channel energy roughly threefold, a replicated power anomaly was resolved by a targeted test to a batching-composition artifact, and an exact repetition returned every headline value inside its registered band. The central claim is bounded and mechanism-indexed: unresolved question-state structure predicts measured physical resolution cost when the resolver instantiates that structure as constraint work, and the cost tracks resolution difficulty, not merely candidate count. The result updates the June ten-gate map by advancing Gate 1 for both exhaustive and pruned search, populating Gate 3b with a hardness-indexed constant on a clean channel, closing Gate 8 at the apparatus layer, and narrowing Gate 9 by separating resolution cost from generation cost.

title: 10 simple rules for hosting sensitive health data securely and privately for research
abstract: It is increasingly common to create “data commons,” “data enclaves,” or “Trusted Research Environments” (TREs) - that is, platforms for hosting consented clinical research data or “real-world data” (RWD) collected under waivers of consent. Such environments aspire to be secure and privacy-preserving, but often fall short of implementing enforceable technical controls or policies that can reliably ensure adequate data protection. This manuscript provides 10 simple rules to protect deeply linked, multimodal health data to help funders, policymakers, IT specialists, research organizations, and investigators who design and deploy enclaves or TREs for sensitive health data.

abstract: ## Abstract h2> We present TRUSTMEM-Hayula, an integrated approach combining TRUSTMEM's trustworthy memory consolidation with EvoTest's evolutionary self-improvement, deployed within the Siyaq context engineering framework. title: Auditing Interpretability Claims for Kolmogorov-Arnold Classification Heads: Reproducibility Code and Results
abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) place learnable univariate B-splines on networkedges and are proposed as interpretable replacements for the multi-layer perceptron(MLP) classification heads that sit atop pretrained backbones in medical imaging.Four claims are made on their behalf: that they cost no accuracy, that theirattributions are faithful, that the extracted curves are reliable across trainingpartitions, and that they transfer. This repository contains the controls those claims had not faced, and what thecontrols show. Applied to diabetic retinopathy grading: - Once head parameter counts are matched, the two heads are **equivalent** in quadratic weighted kappa, established by a two one-sided tests procedure rather than by a failure to reject a null.- Equivalence **survives a frozen backbone** — but only once dropout is placed identically. The reference designs apply dropout to the KAN head's 1280-dimensional input and to the MLP head's 78-dimensional hidden layer, and that asymmetry alone costs the KAN head about 0.03 QWK, enough to be mistaken for an architectural deficit.- Partial-dependence and Integrated Gradients rankings identify the features a trained head relies on, under all three removal operators; a practically-budgeted KernelSHAP does not. **But under remove-and-retrain** (Hooker et al., NeurIPS 2019) no ranking beats a random ordering: a head retrained after half the representation is ablated recovers to within 0.007 QWK.- Spline curves **invert sign** across folds, but the inversions concentrate on low-amplitude curves (Spearman rho = 0.70), so consistency reported as a correlation alone overstates reliability.- On external Messidor-2 the KAN head's AUC advantage is **not significant** across folds (p = 0.073), and blind threshold transfer is unstable for both heads, driven by prevalence shift rather than by miscalibration.

title: Shared Neighbors and Representative Point Assignment-based Spatial–Temporal Density Peaks Clustering
abstract: In spatial–temporal clustering by fast search and find of density peaks, local density definitions often fail to preserve sufficient neighborhood structure, which can lead to the erroneous selection of cluster centers. Furthermore, sample assignment frequently depends solely on the spatial distance between cluster centers, resulting in inadequate spatial–temporal constraints. This limitation often leads to the misclassification of samples that are spatially proximate but exhibit significant differences in their temporal characteristics. To address these issues, this paper proposes a spatial–temporal density peaks clustering (DPC) algorithm based on shared neighbors and representative point assignment (SNRP-STDPC). By adopting a spatial–temporal weighted Euclidean distance as a unified metric and designing a similarity measure based on spatial–temporal shared nearest neighbors (SNN), the algorithm defines a weighted SNN local density to improve the accuracy of cluster center selection. Additionally, a representative point assignment strategy is introduced to identify and isolate uncertain samples. By combining these representative points with SNN similarity, the algorithm achieves precise error correction, ensuring assignment accuracy even under complex data distributions. Experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithm exhibits significant advantages across multiple evaluation metrics.

title: Plaquette: A hardware-aware design platform for fault-tolerant quantum computers
abstract: Hardware teams building fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) must decide which imperfections to suppress, and that decision requires the logical performance of the architecture under the device's actual noise. Hardware noise often departs from the stochastic Pauli models used by scalable stabilizer simulators: superconducting transmons leak out of the computational subspace, neutral atoms scatter through intermediate states, trapped ions heat as their motional modes absorb phonons, and miscalibrated controls over-rotate coherently. We present Plaquette, a theoretical framework and software suite that computes the logical performance of fault-tolerant architectures directly from the physics of such imperfections. In Plaquette, a hardware error model is specified once, as Kraus operators, Hamiltonian-Lindblad dynamics, or an experimentally reconstructed quantum channel, and is compiled automatically into the exact or approximate representation required by each of four sampler classes: stabilizer sampling for Pauli noise, the new XPauli sampler for leakage and environment sectors, near-Clifford samplers for coherent errors, and full-state simulation for exact reference calculations. We validate the XPauli and near-Clifford samplers against full-state simulation, which they can match within statistical uncertainty while Pauli twirling can fall short depending on the error model. We demonstrate the framework on three error models: leakage in superconducting qubits, intermediate-state scattering in neutral atoms, and heating in trapped ions. The size of the discrepancy between Plaquette and Clifford-only simulations varies with platform and noise process, so reliable thresholds, error budgets, and overhead estimates require the most accurate simulation available. Plaquette provides a direct path from the open-system physics of a device to the logical performance of the FTQC built on it.

title: SMetric: Rethink LLM Scheduling for Serving Agents with Balanced Session-centric Scheduling
abstract: LLM scheduling is critical to serving, yet how well existing designs fit agentic serving--where agents, not humans, issue the requests--remains unclear. Agents shift the workload in two ways: they consume many more tokens than humans, so the cluster must provide high throughput (TPS) at low latency; and their requests reuse far more KV\$ than chat. Existing schedulers still trade off load balance against KV\$ reuse: cache-aware schedulers may crowd requests onto the few instances caching the KV\$, leaving the rest idle, while balanced schedulers may lose the opportunity for reuse, which is costly at a high reuse ratio. We thus present two key insights: (1) with a global-tier KV\$ store, pursuing load balance need not compromise KV\$ reuse, though the slower global tier must be used with care; and (2) given the agent's intra-session locality, routing requests by their sessions can balance the load with high KV\$ reuse. A key challenge in realizing session-centric scheduling is that the scheduler must identify a request's session statelessly, which is difficult for model providers serving arbitrary agents. SMetric addresses this with differential scheduling based on two indicators derived from the request itself, the session turn and the local KV\$ hit: it schedules first-turn requests for load balance, and sticks follow-ups to the instance with the highest local hit for high KV\$ reuse. As sessions differ widely in size, SMetric sticks a follow-up only if the instance can serve it within its SLO, and otherwise migrates the session to the least-loaded instance to prevent many long sessions from eventually imbalancing the load. Evaluated on real-world traces, SMetric improves the peak TPS by 9-15% under prefill-decode colocation with a provisioned global tier and the peak prefill TPS by 9% under disaggregation over state-of-the-art schedulers, also with lower latency.

title: Compete Then Collaborate: Frontier AI Teachers Build a Verifiable Curriculum to Improve a Coding Student Beyond Imitation
abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as teachers generating training data for smaller students. Prior multi-teacher knowledge distillation methods merge outputs without determining which frontier model teaches best, often relying on an LLM judge biased toward its own outputs. We introduce a compete-then-collaborate framework where four frontier AI teachers (Claude, Codex-GPT, Grok, Gemini) are ranked head-to-head by an execution-based judge (unit tests and stdin-stdout checks) with fairness controls, and then collaborate to build a verifiable curriculum for a student (Qwen2.5-Coder). We report three findings. (1) Under execution verification, all teachers solve standard problems near-perfectly after self-correction (99-100%) due to a saturation effect, but harder competition problems separate them (Gemini 77% > Claude 69% = Codex 69% > Grok 50%); however, the robust student-side results do not depend on teacher ranking. (2) Imitation (SFT) on verified solutions does not improve, and can degrade, an already-competent student at 7B and 32B (e.g., from 76.7% to 72.7% on MBPP-test, and 5.9% to 2.9% on competition problems). (3) Using the same collaborative curriculum as a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment improves the student (from 5.9% to 8.8% peak on competition problems, a +49% relative gain), reversing SFT's direction. The value of AI-teacher collaboration lies not in pooling answers to imitate, but in jointly constructing a verifiable environment where the student learns by doing. We release a reproducible on-prem pipeline (NVIDIA GB10) with framework patches for running GRPO on a bleeding-edge stack.

title: APIVOT: Adaptive Planning with Interleaved Vision-Language Thoughts
abstract: Long-horizon robot planning requires jointly reasoning over semantic task structure and geometric feasibility. To successfully execute a task, a robot must decompose goals, select task-relevant objects, and sequence actions, while ensuring that plans satisfy spatial constraints such as limited free space and object collisions. In this work, we propose APIVOT, a VLM-based planner that adaptively interleaves language and visual thoughts for long-horizon planning. APIVOT learns to leverage language for semantic reasoning, while using visual thoughts as imagined future states for internal verification of geometric feasibility. On long-horizon kitchen tasks, APIVOT outperforms general-purpose VLMs and prior planning frameworks, achieving the largest gains in spatially constrained settings. We find that APIVOT learns meaningful modality selection behavior, demonstrating that adaptive interleaving of vision-language thoughts improves both planning success and reasoning efficiency.

title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Credit Card Application Approval
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Credit Card Application ApprovalThis dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_47 dataset, derived from the Credit Card Applications Dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository - CRX). The original data comprises 15 anonymized attributes (A1 through A15) describing credit card applications, with a mix of continuous, binary, and nominal categorical variables. All attribute names and values have been replaced with meaningless symbols to protect data confidentiality. The target variable (originally A16) indicates whether a credit card application was approved (+) or rejected (-), mapped to target (1 = Approved, 0 = Rejected).Generation and Selection Methodology: The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where a suitable technique was selected), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the SMOTE RSB + Ruido Gaussiano* algorithm, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (9.928) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating near-perfect preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 9,978 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 16 (15 predictive features + 1 target variable)Target Variable: target (1 = Credit approved, 0 = Credit rejected)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 1.207).Intended Use: This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for credit risk assessment, credit scoring, and automated credit decision-making in the banking and financial services industry. It is suitable for training and evaluating binary classification algorithms where accurate prediction of credit approval is critical for operational efficiency and risk management. The synthetic nature of the data allows for safe sharing and benchmarking without exposing potentially sensitive financial information. The anonymized nature of the attributes (A1-A15) makes this dataset particularly valuable for evaluating algorithmic performance without domain-specific bias.Performance Summary: Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.84, AUC-ROC of 0.96, and accuracy of 0.84. The original model showed excellent performance on both classes, with precision of 0.82 and recall of 0.83 for the minority class (approved). Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.98 (+0.14 improvement), AUC-ROC of 1.00 (+0.04 improvement), and accuracy of 0.98 (+0.14 improvement). The synthetic data significantly improved the minority class performance, increasing precision from 0.82 to 1.00 (+0.18), recall from 0.83 to 0.97 (+0.14), and F1-score from 0.82 to 0.98 (+0.16). This demonstrates the exceptional effectiveness of the methodology in capturing complex credit approval patterns and achieving near-perfect classification performance.Data Preprocessing Note: The original dataset (690 credit applications) was obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Missing values represented by '?' were treated as NaN. Rows with missing values were removed (approximately 5% of the data) to ensure data integrity. The target variable (A16) was renamed to target and mapped from '+' (Approved) to 1 and '-' (Rejected) to 0. All categorical variables (A1, A4, A5, A6, A7, A9, A10, A12, A13) were label-encoded using cat.codes with complete mapping documentation provided in the accompanying legend file (leyenda_credit_approval.txt). Numerical variables (A2, A3, A8, A11, A14, A15) were preserved in their original numeric format. All variables were converted to appropriate numeric types for consistency.Privacy and Ethics: The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real credit applications that could be traced to specific individuals. The original dataset is already fully anonymized with all attribute names and values replaced by meaningless symbols (A1-A16). The synthetic generation process ensures that no real individual can be re-identified. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). evidence.title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Credit Card Application Approval
evidence.abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Credit Card Application ApprovalThis dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_47 dataset, derived from the Credit Card Applications Dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository - CRX). The original data comprises 15 anonymized attributes (A1 through A15) describing credit card applications, with a mix of continuous, binary, and nominal categorical variables. All attribute names and values have been replaced with meaningless symbols to protect data confidentiality. The target variable (originally A16) indicates whether a credit card application was approved (+) or rejected (-), mapped to target (1 = Approved, 0 = Rejected).Generation and Selection Methodology: The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where a suitable technique was selected), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the SMOTE RSB + Ruido Gaussiano* algorithm, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (9.928) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating near-perfect preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 9,978 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 16 (15 predictive features + 1 target variable)Target Variable: target (1 = Credit approved, 0 = Credit rejected)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 1.207).Intended Use: This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for credit risk assessment, credit scoring, and automated credit decision-making in the banking and financial services industry. title: Automated reinforcement learning for intelligent maneuver decision-making in unmanned aerial vehicles
abstract: Intelligent maneuver decision-making is perceived as a pivotal component in the evolution of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) technology. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL), an advanced intelligent algorithm, furnishes substantial support for the execution of intelligent maneuver decision-making in UAVs. Nevertheless, DRL encounters substantial challenges when dealing with high-dimensional continuous state and action spaces, intricate unknown environments, and sparse rewards. In previous research, scholars have frequently simplified the maneuver decision-making process by discretizing the action space, an approach that is incompatible with real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an automatic curriculum reinforcement learning (ACRL) training framework that incorporates the Proximal Policy Optimization with clipped objective (PPO-clip) algorithm, aiming to tackle the inefficiencies and ineffectiveness inherent in traditional UAV maneuver decision-making training methodologies. Drawing inspiration from the human learning process, which evolves from simple to complex, we partition the entire maneuver decision-making training process into a series of sub-curricula, each escalating in difficulty. Self-play game simulation experiments within the line of sight (LOS) range demonstrate that the UAV iteratively optimizes its strategy as it completes these sub-curricula. We validate the effectiveness and applicability of our method by comparing its training outcomes with those without a curriculum.

title: Inference, Inferential Goodness, and Logic
abstract: Abstract This chapter begins by developing a skeletal framework for thinking about the nature and structure of deductive inference, drawing on insights from numerous philosophers who have commented on the nature of this mental activity over the course of millennia. The chapter then turns to describe how an activity like formal logic could be seen as investigating the conditions under which the mental activity of deductive inference is performed well or correctly. Special attention is paid to how inference’s status as a goodness-fixing kind makes room for logic to investigate its attendant standard of goodness in a limited, but productive way.

title: Advancing Health Equity through Multi-Level Fairness in Health Informatics
abstract: The increasing integration of machine learning in healthcare has highlighted critical challenges related to fairness, transparency, and health equity. Specifically, the use of multi-level fairness techniques, which combine multiple bias mitigation steps or techniques, show promise for reducing biases across different patient demographics, yet this approach remains underexplored in terms of its health equity outcomes. In this paper, we assess the current landscape of multi-level fairness in health informatics by focusing on its impact on equitable healthcare outcomes and evaluating how transparency and reporting standards contribute to these advancements. Through an examination of the existing literature, we identify key gaps in both the implementation of multi-level fairness techniques and the consistent reporting of health equity impacts. Furthermore, we analyze the role of reporting standards, including MINIMAR and TRIPOD, in improving model transparency and ensuring that machine learning models in healthcare address health disparities. These standards offer valuable benchmarks for reporting on ML models, yet we identify key opportunities for enhancing how these reports capture fairness and equity outcomes. The paper concludes by providing recommendations that focus on improving transparency in reporting, advocating for the broader adoption of multi-level fairness techniques, and ensuring that health equity is explicitly prioritized in future research efforts.

title: QMA Lower Bounds for Batch Verification via Approximate Degree
abstract: We study batch verification in QMA query and communication complexity, where the goal is to understand how the resources needed to verify $m$ copies of a Boolean function $f$ depend on $m$. We give a general technique for proving lower bounds on the witness-query tradeoff needed to batch verify a function $f$ in terms of its approximate degree. Applying this technique to an explicit family of DNF formulas $f$, we show that attempting to save even a constant factor on the witness length of the baseline approach to batch verifying $f$ necessitates a large polynomial increase in the query cost. We also obtain new lower bounds on the QMA query complexity of read-once CNF formulas and on the surjectivity and $k$-element distinctness functions. Our lower bounds also lift to give communication analogs of these results.

title: CASL-VAE: Learning Structured Latent Variables from Unpaired Data for Semi-supervised Clustering and Paired Sample Generation
abstract: Quantifying variability in a target population relative to a reference population is central to many scientific and clinical problems (e.g., diseased vs. healthy). Yet, without paired data and in the presence of heterogeneous target variation, existing methods struggle to separate multiple modes of target-specific variation. We propose \textit{CASL-VAE}, a deep contrastive latent variable model that learns structured latent generative factors from unpaired data. CASL-VAE factorizes variation into continuous common latent factors shared across populations and hierarchical salient latent factors that model target-specific heterogeneity as discrete subtypes and continuous within-subtype variation. Using variational inference, we show how approximate joint likelihood optimization over reference and target domains can be performed using unpaired data, providing a principled basis for paired-sample generation and cross-domain analysis. We validate CASL-VAE on semi-synthetic neuroimaging data, demonstrating improved subtype recovery and paired-sample generation compared to baseline clustering and generative models. We also validate its ability to reveal biologically plausible heterogeneity in Alzheimer's disease.

title: From Bayes' Rule to Bayes Rules: Optimal Information Processing and Axiomatic Foundations Beyond Probability
abstract: This paper develops principled updating rules for possibilistic inference, where uncertainty about a fixed parameter is represented by a possibility function, the maxitive analogue of a probability distribution, and comparisons are made pointwise via a partial order. From two complementary foundations, an information-conservation viewpoint and an axiomatic viewpoint, we derive the same canonical update: the posterior is the prior-likelihood product followed by supremum normalisation. The two derivations agree for an arbitrary loss, differing only in where the learning-rate parameter enters. This parameter controls epistemic strength and is not identifiable from the normalising evidence alone, clarifying the role of analogous learning-rate parameters in generalised Bayesian updating.
